title: Hyperparameter Tuning — Diagnosing and Fixing a Poor Fit
description: A damped oscillation dataset (y = e^(−0.6x₁)·cos(4πx₁) + 0.8x₂² − 0.4x₂) produces a characteristic S-curve residual pattern when trained with default GPR settings. You will read the residual plot to diagnose the failure mode, use the Kernel & Hyperparameter Guide decision tree to select the right fix, then compare manual tuning against the auto-tune result.

steps.instruction: The dataset has 2 inputs and 1 output. x1 drives a damped oscillation (the response oscillates and shrinks as x1 increases); x2 drives a smooth quadratic trend. The default GPR kernel (RBF) assumes infinite smoothness — it will over-smooth the oscillatory x1 component.

quiz.question: The response contains e^(−0.6x₁)·cos(4πx₁) — an exponentially damped cosine. The envelope shrinks and the frequency is fixed. Which part of this expression would the RBF kernel struggle with most?
options: The exponential decay e^(−0.6x₁) — GPR cannot model decaying responses
The cosine oscillation cos(4πx₁) — RBF assumes smooth monotone correlation decay, not periodic sign changes in the response
The interaction with x₂ — GPR cannot model additive components
The fixed frequency — GPR can only model variable-frequency responses
quiz.explanation: Exponential decay is smooth and monotone — GPR handles it well. The oscillatory cos(4πx₁) forces the response to change direction every 0.25 units of x₁. RBF kernel correlation between points 0.5 units apart is still positive (correlated), but the true response is anti-correlated at that lag. This mismatch causes the kernel to over-smooth, missing the oscillation peaks.

steps.instruction: Designate x1 and x2 as inputs and y as the output.
Apply Min-Max normalization to both inputs.

Train a GPR with all defaults — RBF kernel, alpha = 0.1, test split 0.2, 5 CV folds. Note the R² and open the residual plot. Look carefully at the residual vs. predicted values — you should see an S-curve (systematic curvature), not random scatter.

quiz.question: The residual plot shows an S-shaped curve: low predicted values have positive residuals and high predicted values have negative residuals (or vice versa). What is the most likely cause?
options: The dataset contains outliers that are skewing the residuals
The model is systematically underpredicting peaks and overpredicting troughs — a sign the kernel is too smooth and is missing curvature in the response
The test split was set too low
Normalization was not applied
quiz.explanation: An S-curve in the residual plot is a classic symptom of kernel mismatch: the model's smoothness assumption is too strong for the actual response. The model sees high true values (oscillation peaks) as 'too extreme' given its smooth prior, so it predicts lower values — creating positive residuals at peaks. The opposite happens at troughs. The S-shape traces the model's systematic bias across the response range.

steps.instruction: Open the Guide → Kernel & Hyperparameter Guide. Follow the decision tree for 'oscillatory or rough response'. It will recommend Matérn1.5 or Matérn2.5. Switch the GPR kernel to Matérn2.5 and retrain. Check whether the S-curve disappears from the residual plot and R² improves.

quiz.question: After switching to Matérn2.5, the residual S-curve largely disappears and R² improves. What does this confirm?
options: Matérn2.5 is always better than RBF
The original poor fit was caused by a kernel mismatch — the RBF smoothness assumption was wrong for this data. Matérn2.5's weaker assumption better matches the actual response character
The dataset had an error that was corrected by retraining
More CV folds would have fixed the RBF result without changing the kernel
quiz.explanation: A systematic residual pattern that vanishes when you change the kernel confirms the original failure was the model prior, not the data or settings. This is the diagnostic value of the residual plot: random scatter = good fit; systematic pattern = structural mismatch. The Kernel Guide maps residual patterns to recommended fixes — this is the intended workflow.

steps.instruction: Now try increasing alpha from 0.1 to 0.5 with the Matérn2.5 kernel still selected. Alpha adds noise regularization to the GPR diagonal — it controls the trade-off between interpolation (alpha near 0) and smoothing (alpha large). Retrain and compare the residual plot.

quiz.question: Increasing alpha from 0.1 to 0.5 reduces R² slightly but makes the residual plot smoother and the CV score more consistent. When is a higher alpha preferable despite the lower R²?
options: Never — R² should always be maximised
When the training data has measurement noise or the CV score is unstable, a higher alpha prevents the model from fitting noise, giving more reliable predictions on new data
When the dataset has more than 100 rows
When using Matérn kernels instead of RBF
quiz.explanation: Alpha acts as a noise floor: the model is told that observations have variance alpha², so it does not try to pass exactly through every training point. Very low alpha (near-interpolation) fits training data tightly but may chase measurement noise, degrading generalisation. If CV folds show high score variance (some folds score much lower than others), that is a sign the model is overfitting; increasing alpha usually stabilises CV performance.

steps.instruction: Finally, reset to Matérn2.5 with the original alpha = 0.1 and click 'Auto-Tune →'. Auto-tune runs a grid search over kernel, alpha, and optimizer restarts. Compare its chosen configuration against what the Kernel Guide decision tree recommended manually. They should agree on kernel but may differ on alpha.

quiz.question: Auto-tune selects the configuration that maximises CV R². A human reading the Kernel Guide made the same kernel recommendation but a different alpha choice. Which approach is more reliable?
options: Auto-tune is always more reliable — it searches systematically over many combinations
The Kernel Guide is always more reliable — it encodes domain knowledge

They are complementary: the Kernel Guide quickly rules out wrong kernel families (faster than a grid search); auto-tune then fine-tunes numeric parameters like alpha within the correct kernel. Using both beats either alone
Whichever achieves higher test R² is more reliable
quiz.explanation: A grid search over all kernels and all alpha values is comprehensive but slow. The Kernel Guide shortcut — look at the residual pattern, identify the smoothness mismatch, pick the kernel — reduces the search space dramatically. Auto-tune then optimises within that reduced space. In practice: use the Guide to choose the kernel family, then auto-tune to find the best numeric settings. This hybrid approach is faster and more principled than blind grid search.
